title: DBSCAN & Density-based Clustering
interviewAnswer: DBSCAN defines clusters as dense regions connected through neighborhoods, can identify noise points, and does not require a fixed number of clusters. It struggles when cluster densities vary strongly.
why: DBSCAN & Density-based Clustering appears frequently in data-science work because it connects mathematical assumptions to practical decisions, diagnostics and failure modes.
deepDive: DBSCAN defines clusters as dense regions connected through neighborhoods, can identify noise points, and does not require a fixed number of clusters. It struggles when cluster densities vary strongly. Scaling/distance choice matters. Can find non-spherical clusters. A strong practitioner separates the modeling assumption from the estimation procedure, checks diagnostics rather than trusting a single score, and explains what would make the method inappropriate.
workedExample: Detect spatial event clusters while labeling isolated coordinates as noise.
commonMistakes: Applying the method without checking its assumptions or data-generating process.
Choosing it because it is familiar rather than comparing against an appropriate baseline.
followUps: What assumptions does DBSCAN & Density-based Clustering make?
How would you validate or debug DBSCAN & Density-based Clustering in practice?
production: In production, validate assumptions on real data, monitor the quantities that can drift, and keep a simple baseline so added complexity has a measurable reason to exist.

lab.goal: Recover density-based clusters and noise points.
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
Z=StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
labels=DBSCAN(eps=.25,min_samples=6).fit_predict(Z)
print('clusters',set(labels),'noise',(labels==-1).sum())
lab.shipIt: Scale features consistently and tune eps/min_samples against domain meaning; do not treat noise labels as automatically fraudulent or wrong.
